data.title: Tawhid and the Five Pillars
data.sourcePassage: The most fundamental belief in Islam is tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah. Muslims believe that God is utterly unique, without partner, equal, or rival. This belief shapes everything in Muslim life, from worship to art to ethics. The Five Pillars of Islam are the core acts of worship that every Muslim is expected to perform, and they flow from this belief in tawhid. The Shahadah declares faith in the one God. Salah connects Muslims to God five times every day. Zakah requires sharing wealth with those in need. Sawm involves fasting during Ramadan to develop self-discipline and empathy. Hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca that unites millions of Muslims worldwide. Together, the Five Pillars express belief in one God through practical daily action.

data.title: The Mosque and Community Worship
data.sourcePassage: The mosque — or masjid in Arabic, meaning 'place of prostration' — is the Muslim place of worship and community centre. Every mosque has several key features. The mihrab is a niche in the wall that shows the direction of Mecca (qiblah), so worshippers know which way to face during Salah. The minbar is a raised platform from which the imam delivers the Friday sermon called the khutbah. There is a wudu area where Muslims perform ritual washing before prayer. The prayer hall has no images of God or humans — reflecting tawhid and the belief that God is beyond any physical representation. Instead, walls are often decorated with geometric patterns and Arabic calligraphy from the Qur'an. On Fridays, Muslims gather for Jumu'ah — the communal midday prayer — which strengthens the sense of ummah.

data.title: Ramadan and Eid
data.sourcePassage: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar and a time of great spiritual significance. Muslims believe the Qur'an was first revealed to Muhammad during this month. During Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset — abstaining from food, drink, and other things. Before dawn, they eat the Suhoor meal; at sunset, they break the fast with Iftar, often starting with dates and water following the Prophet's example. Beyond fasting, Ramadan involves increased prayer, Qur'an reading, and charitable giving. The Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in the last ten days is considered the most holy night of the year. At the end of Ramadan comes Eid al-Fitr — the Festival of Breaking the Fast. Muslims attend a special morning prayer, give Zakat al-Fitr so the poor can celebrate, wear their best clothes, and share meals with family and community.
